problem: Conventional navigation assumes a feasible path exists in a fixed free workspace, and NAMO methods only remove obstacles (not use them as tools). Existing LLM TAMP methods need omniscient scene descriptions, plan open-loop, or replan only after failure.
motivation: In disaster zones or cluttered warehouses no path may exist a priori, so the robot must change the workspace (push boxes, build stairs) using only egocentric, incrementally revealed observations. Planning must therefore be robust to LLM errors and adapt to new objects and changed affordances, not just failures.
key_idea: Use an LLM to build a primitive skill tree (object-level then skill-level plans, scored by an LLM evaluator) executed by RL-pretrained quadruped skills, with an advisor LLM deciding when to replan and an arborist LLM adding or pruning tree nodes.
insight: Multiple alternative plans in a tree, plus going from object-level reasoning to skill-level steps, make planning more robust than a single LLM plan. Ablations (middle/high difficulty maze tasks, shown in a figure only) find that AINav-Single, AINav-Skill, AINav-No and AINav-F all do worse than full AINav. Failure-only replanning (AINav-F) misses new useful objects and wastes time. The failure study shows the remaining bottlenecks are incorrect task decomposition (34.5%) and unfinished skill execution (24.1%).
method: Perception input: CLIP as VLM for scene understanding (e.g. whether paths are blocked) and YOLOv8 for object detection with position and size; the robot is assumed to know which objects are movable.

Proposer (LLM_p): first proposes five object-level strategies, then converts them to skill-level plans over the library (walk, climb, navigate, push); plans are merged by shared prefixes into a primitive skill tree.

Evaluator (LLM_e): scores each node's immediate reward in [0,1] by task contribution and skill difficulty; non-executable nodes and their subtrees are deleted; a terminal bonus is given at goal-reaching leaves; Q(n)=r(n)+γ·mean Q(children) is backpropagated, and the child with maximal Q is selected greedily.

RL skill library: PPO in IsaacLab; walking (velocity tracking) and climbing (goal reaching, move-direction reward, head-collision penalty, terrain/hurdle curriculum) are low-level; navigation and pushing are hierarchical-RL pose-tracking skills that issue velocity commands, trained with randomized box shapes and obstacle density.
Advisor (LLM): interprets new observations as failure, new object or revaluation, then decides whether replanning would improve on the current plan and writes suggestions.

Arborist (LLM): applies the advisor's suggestions by adding nodes for new objects and pruning failed or infeasible paths, followed by backpropagation and re-selection of the skeleton; symbolic parameters are converted to coordinates by an LLM.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) for proposer/evaluator/advisor/arborist; CLIP as VLM; YOLOv8 detector; PPO-trained RL skill policies for Unitree Go2
setting.training_data: RL skills trained in IsaacLab simulation with curricula and domain randomization (no external data); LLMs used zero-shot via prompts
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB (CLIP/YOLOv8), lidar height map for skills; in simulation noisy object dimensions are provided; in real-world tests AprilTag gives object pose/size and SLAM Toolbox gives robot pose
setting.action_space: Discrete primitive skills with parameters (walk, climb, navigate, push with target position/object id) executed as joint control by RL policies
setting.simulator: IsaacSim / IsaacLab (maze, Matterport3D, urban ruin, field ruin)
setting.privileged: Robot knows whether visible objects are movable or fixed; simulation uses noisy object dimensions instead of real perception; real-world uses AprilTags for object pose and dimension

results: AINav reaches the highest SR in every simulated scenario, e.g. 90% in Matterport vs 50% for Tree-planner and 30% for RoboTool, and 90% on box obstruction H vs 60% (Tree-planner) and 30% (RoboTool). Art-planner and hierarchical RL fail on all interactive tasks. In real-world tests AINav averages 64% SR vs 36% for RoboTool.
limitations: Relies on simplified perception (noisy GT dimensions in simulation, AprilTags in real world) and predefined constraints for skill executability.

Failures are dominated by incorrect task decomposition (34.5%) and unfinished skill execution (24.1%), plus skill-transition failures; real-world stair building only 20% SR due to execution on non-fixed boxes.
Small trial counts (10 in simulation, 5 real) and a limited skill set (walk, climb, navigate, push).
